title: Teaching on Purpose #16 Providing Practice, Consolidation and Feedback
author: Adam Kohlbeck
summary: The sixteenth installment of Kohlbeck's series on Chiltern Learning Trust's six core purposes of teaching, drawing on his podcast conversation with English teacher Yamina Bibi about practice, consolidation and feedback. His central claim is that accountability pressure pushes teachers to design practice that produces an artefact, and that the artefact is the wrong target because the value of practice lies in how it makes students think with what they have been taught. He presses the point with an Early Years example, a Reception water tray where paper boats disintegrate and the teacher asks whether the material or the folding is responsible, then produces alternative materials from a cupboard as children name them. The same example is then used to dissolve the apparent opposition between detailed planning and responsive teaching, since the teacher's improvised questioning only worked because the materials had been prepared in advance. He goes on to correct a common misreading of I do, we do, you do as a timetabled lesson structure rather than a sequence a teacher moves back and forth through, and answers the standard objection about split readiness by splitting the class. The final section argues that the retreat from written marking has been both a workload win and a learning gain, and proposes a per-lesson assessment booklet in which circulating teachers log which student held which misconception.
points: Kohlbeck distinguishes evidence of learning from evidence of teaching and performance, arguing the second is usually what a produced artefact actually shows.
The Reception boat episode is chosen precisely because it yields no artefact at all, which isolates thinking as the thing practice is for.
He reframes detailed team and curriculum planning as the precondition of responsive teaching rather than its opposite, since the cupboard had to be stocked beforehand.
I do, we do, you do is described as a sequence that may repeat or reverse within a lesson, not a set of allocated time slots some schools now mandate.
The proposed replacement for marking is a lesson-by-lesson booklet recording who held which misconception, so the record can be revisited and the next lesson retuned.
quotes: The inverted commas here are deliberate because often, while we might say ‘evidence of learning’, what we actually mean can be closer to ‘evidence of teaching and performance’.
The true value of the practice is in how it enables students to think about and with what they have been taught.

The children noticed that the paper kept getting wet and the boats fell apart. The teacher asked if they thought it was the material that caused the boat to fall apart or if it was how the paper had been folded.

Sometimes this can feel like the antithesis of the kind of responsive teaching that we hold up as the end goal of teaching expertise development. Far from it being that, it is in fact a necessary foundation that allows adaption.
But… the other materials had been strategically prepared before the lesson and were on hand in the cupboard when the children mentioned them.

This is not a lesson structure. It is a sequence that may be repeated multiple times in a lesson or may involve the teacher moving back and forth between depending on the evidence of student understanding that they collect.
This has lead to a rare workload victory for teachers but it has also improved student learning by shifting teachers’ mindsets from performative marking to purposeful feedback.
Teachers carry the booklet around the room with them as they circulate, noting down misconceptions that they come across.
